source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: 201 Japanese wordplay riddles that need restructuring. Most of 38 LLMs are far below humans in a strict zero-shot, no-retrieval test.
numbers: Human mean 52.9% (n=126, 120-item subset). Non-reasoning models mean 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. Full 201 items: 9.42% vs 19.25%. Only GPT-5 fell inside the human 95% CI.
limits: Wordplay in Japanese; grading by gold-answer variants; human sample is a pilot survey; descriptive overlap is not statistical equivalence.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-model gains on insight items are real but small. A scaffold should not assume the base model can restructure.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Verification failure: the model writes the correct answer in its thought log, then does not commit and answers wrongly.
numbers: Share of incorrect answers that were verification failures: Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview 5.23%, Claude Opus 4 25.00%, DeepSeek-R1-0528 30.57%, Grok 4 39.34% (literal match of gold variant in log before final line).
quote: models generate a correct intermediate candidate but fail to endorse it as their final answer
limits: Literal string matching only; 4 models with usable logs; automated accuracy differs from main scoring.
agent_relevance: Strong case for an explicit candidate ledger and commit step: keep every candidate seen, and pick by a check, not by the last thought.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Parameter count did not predict accuracy; release date did. Language of the thought log (English vs Japanese) gave inconsistent effects.
numbers: Grok-4: English 48.8% (40/82) vs Japanese 29.5% (33/112), Fisher p=0.0071. Claude Opus 4: 28.7% vs 36.7%, p=0.356. Overall: DeepSeek-R1-0528 22.9%, Gemini-2.5-flash-preview 10.9%, Claude-opus-4 30.3%, Grok-4 37.6%.
limits: Per-model language use is self-selected by the model, so not a clean experiment.
agent_relevance: Surface language switching is not a lever; do not add it.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) The Metacognitive Bottleneck: Japanese Riddles (NazoNazo Benchmark)
finding: Authors also describe a false-insight pattern: the model commits with confidence to a wrong reframing. Item difficulty is skewed for LLMs (most items very hard) but spread normally for humans.
numbers: Human scores bimodal, consistent with insight literature; LLM per-item correct rate skewed low (descriptive, no single number).
limits: Qualitative; analogy to human false aha (Danek and Wiley 2017) is descriptive, not mechanistic.
agent_relevance: Two opposite failure modes need two guards: failure to commit, and over-commit to a wrong frame (independent check).

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Mid-trace Aha shifts in RL-trained reasoning models are rare, do not grow with training, and usually coincide with lower accuracy.
numbers: Over 11M traces, 4 temperatures (0, 0.05, 0.3, 0.7), 20 checkpoints. Shifts in about 6.31% of traces; formal Aha criteria met in 1.79%. Pooled Qwen2.5-1.5B accuracy 2.57% with a shift vs 16.44% without (N=723,200). MATH-500: 14.4% vs 32.7%. Crosswords exception: 20.1% vs 9.6%.
quote: rare, do not become more frequent with training
limits: Lexical detection of shifts; three verifiable domains (Cryptonite crosswords, MATH-500, 6x6 Rush Hour); mainly Qwen and Llama families, small models.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous wait-actually is a symptom of trouble, not a repair. Do not rely on free-running reconsideration.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Externally triggered reconsideration under high uncertainty (entropy) helps; spontaneous shifts under high entropy do not.
numbers: Triggered reconsideration on Math: 32.2% to 40.6% (+8.41 pp; wins 50,574 vs losses 23,500). Crosswords +0.45 pp (wins 5,380 vs losses 5,004). Rush Hour +0.01 pp. Training-stage marginal effect on Math -0.0615 (p=1.55e-4).
limits: Prompt-level intervention; says nothing about internal mechanism; gain is domain dependent and almost zero on crosswords.
agent_relevance: Supports a gated restructure operator: fire reconsideration when uncertainty is high (e.g. sample disagreement), not on every step.

source: d'Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Larger or stronger models shift even less; the shift judge was reliable.
numbers: DeepSeek-R1 on MATH-500 shifts 0.00 to 0.25%; GPT-4o 0.88 to 2.21%, with lower accuracy at every temperature when a shift occurs. GPT-4o judge kappa about 0.726 across prompts, 0.79 vs human majority.
limits: Judge is an LLM; 3 domains.
agent_relevance: Do not count Aha tokens as evidence of restructuring when scoring our agent.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Tests Einstellung-style mental set on DeCaro (2016) math-equivalence problems: complex problems first or shortcut problems first, 6 problems per condition.
numbers: Few-shot exact match (SP, SP+CPF, CP, CP+SPF): Llama-3.1-8B 0.16/0/0/0; Llama-3.1-70B 0/0.16/0/0.66; GPT-4o 0.33/0.66/0.66/0.83. With zero-shot CoT added: GPT-4o 0.66/0.66/0.83/0.83. Steps stay 1 under few-shot but 3 with CoT.
limits: Tiny: 6 items per cell, so each item is 0.16. 5-page preprint, no stats. Order effect is not clean: complex-first often helped, the opposite of human set.
agent_relevance: Weak evidence. CoT forced 3-step solutions where a one-step shortcut existed, so CoT may itself induce a procedural set.

source: Haq et al. (2025) Is your LLM trapped in a Mental Set?
finding: Authors read the CoT step count as a sign of mental set: humans use one step on shortcut items, LLMs used more than one when CoT was on.
numbers: Steps equal 3 for all three models under few-shot + zero-shot CoT; 1 under plain few-shot for successful cases.
limits: Interpretation is the authors; no human comparison run in the paper.
agent_relevance: Instruct the agent to try the cheapest representation first, then escalate.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Multiple-choice lateral-thinking puzzles (sentence and word) with semantic and context reconstructions to detect memorization.
numbers: About 1.1K items. Human experts about 92% (91.98 sentence, 91.67 word; 102 sampled questions). Best model ChatGPT 62.68 sentence, 53.46 word. Random 25%.
limits: Multiple choice with four options; ChatGPT may have seen some word puzzles; licence limits.
agent_relevance: Old baseline; later models probably higher, so use it only as a floor.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for Large Language Models
finding: Models are inconsistent across rewrites of the same puzzle, so part of the score is memorization and misleading commonsense.
numbers: ChatGPT and RoBERTa-L fail 45% and 61% of original or semantic-variant puzzles whose context-reconstructed version they answer right. Human group accuracy barely drops.
limits: Group-based metric needs all three variants right.
agent_relevance: Evaluate our agent on rewrites, not only the original item.

source: Sadeghi et al. (2024) uTeBC-NLP at SemEval-2024 Task 9: Can LLMs be Lateral Thinkers?
finding: Prompt study on the BrainTeaser sentence-puzzle task with GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Zephyr-7B: CoT, task hints, RAG few-shot.
numbers: Post-evaluation scores range from 15% (weak configs) to 97.5% (best GPT-4 config); GPT-3.5 rows 57.5 to 75; compressed informative hints beat both no hint and long hints in several settings.
limits: Table is a mixed submission log; single run per config; scores move in steps of 2.5 (40 items); not a controlled ablation.
agent_relevance: Short, targeted hints about the trick types help; longer prompts hurt. Keep restructure prompts short.

source: Sadeghi et al. (2024) uTeBC-NLP at SemEval-2024 Task 9: Can LLMs be Lateral Thinkers?
finding: Fine-tuning Zephyr-7B on lateral-thinking reasoning paths raised scores on other commonsense sets.
numbers: SWAG 38 to 46 and CSQA 31.33 to 36 after tuning (table rows; column mapping approximate).
limits: Small model; unclear column mapping in the extracted table; no replication.
agent_relevance: Lateral thinking traces may transfer, but this is weak and was not run on a strong model.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Weak-eval-Strong: SPLAT, Situation Puzzles for Lateral Thinking
finding: 975 graded situation puzzles in a multi-turn player-judge game: the model asks questions of a judge to infer the hidden story.
numbers: Average accuracy: GPT-4 41.70%, WizardLM-2 35.45%, Llama3-70B 34.50%, GPT-4 Turbo 32.91%, Qwen1.5-110B 29.19%, Llama3-8B 17.05%. GPT-4 easy 70.96%, medium 36.88%, hard 17.27%. Average rounds 11.77 for GPT-4. Judge agrees with humans over 80%.
limits: Judge is an LLM; models are 2024.
agent_relevance: This is a questioning game, close to a hypothesis-by-question operator; accuracy falls steeply as the reframing gets less guessable.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Weak-eval-Strong: SPLAT, Situation Puzzles for Lateral Thinking
finding: Using SPLAT questions and reasoning traces as prompts raised other lateral benchmarks.
numbers: RiddleSense: Llama3-8B 70.51 to 72.18, Llama3-70B 83.34 to 85.21, GPT-4 88.83 to 89.23. BrainTeaser avg: Llama3-8B 61.45 to 66.71, Llama3-70B 80.76 to 85.42 (data plus reasoning prompts).
limits: Gains are 0.4 to 5 points on single runs; GPT-4 gain small.
agent_relevance: Modest, positive; question-asking traces help weaker models more than strong ones.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: 1,600+ everyday problems built to force unconventional tool use (functional fixedness). Humans and GPT-4 fail in different ways.
numbers: GPT-4 efficient solution rate 18.9%, infeasible 37.5%. Majority-vote correct: humans 79.3%, GPT-4 73.3%. Humans bimodal (perfect or total fail); GPT-4 in the middle.
limits: 78% solvable and 22% unsolvable by design; LLM-generated problems; crowd-worker humans.
agent_relevance: The main LLM failure is physical infeasibility, not fixation. A feasibility check beats a novelty push.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Error analysis of GPT-4: most errors are wrong tool use or breaking a stated constraint.
numbers: Wrong tool usage 42.4% of errors, not achieving the goal 17.7%, unnecessary steps 16.9%, using unavailable tools 9.5% (26.4% constraint-related).
limits: Single error taxonomy over a sample.
agent_relevance: Add a step that re-reads constraints and lists available objects before accepting a plan.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver: Are Large Language Models Creative Problem Solvers?
finding: Two scaffolds on 180 solvable problems: iterative step-wise reflection (checks feasibility) and divergent-convergent thinking (generate many, then pick).
numbers: GPT-4: self-reflect cut infeasible solutions by 9.7 points and div-conv by 4.3; div-conv raised efficient solutions by 6.5 points, self-reflect by 2.2. Claude2 and Llama2-13B did not gain from self-reflect (Llama2 always says its answer is wrong); div-conv helped all three.
limits: One sample of 180; zero-shot; no significance tests.
agent_relevance: Div-conv is the safer operator for weaker backbones; reflection works only with a strong model and a concrete target (feasibility).

source: Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: 618 Only Connect walls: sort 16 clues into 4 groups with deliberate red herrings. Mimics RAT with Einstellung.
numbers: On 494 test walls, GPT-4 10-shot solved 6 walls and 239 groups; GPT-3.5 10-shot solved 0 walls and 140 groups. Best embedding model solved 0 walls. Human connection accuracy 80% vs best model about 41 to 45% F1.
limits: Connection scoring by ROUGE/BERTScore; GPT-4 only, 2023.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM test of fixation by distractors; the best model still solves about 1% of walls.

source: Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are Fixated by Red Herrings (Only Connect Wall)
finding: Removing red herrings raises performance a lot, supporting the fixation account.
numbers: GPT-4 10-shot: OCW-WordNet (no red herrings) 471 solved walls and 1,926 correct groups; OCW-Randomized 59 walls and 595 groups; original OCW 6 walls and 239 groups.
limits: Synthetic variants differ in more than red herrings (easier clusters); not a pure manipulation.
agent_relevance: Distractor pressure is a first-order difficulty; the agent should name the obvious grouping and deliberately test alternatives to it.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o vs humans on Chinese insight tasks and RAT: models beat humans on outcomes.
numbers: RAT (30 items): all three models more accurate than humans (GPT-4o +0.35, GPT-4 +0.26, GPT-3.5 +0.19 regression estimate, all p<0.001; 61 instances per model). Insight: GPT-4o beat humans on character puzzles (+0.21), stumpers (+0.06) and rebus (+0.39); GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were below humans on character puzzles (-0.09) and stumpers (-0.20, -0.06).
limits: Chinese-language items; model instances are repeated API calls, not independent people; contamination not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Final-answer scores hide process: strong on classic insight items, which may be memorized.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Process test: on a representational-change (rebus) task, humans beat the models and use a different strategy.
numbers: Humans higher accuracy than GPT-4-turbo (+0.46) and GPT-4o (+0.31), p<0.001. Strategy in correct trials: models used reasoning 68.88% (4o) and 71.26% (turbo); humans used transformation 72.41%.
limits: Image plus description task with four options; two models; coding by 3 raters (alpha 0.88).
agent_relevance: Models reach answers by deduction rather than reframing; keep an explicit reframe operator instead of relying on emergent insight.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) AI Delivers Creative Output but Struggles with Thinking Processes
finding: Models wrong answers on RAT stay closer to the stimulus words than humans wrong answers.
numbers: Relative semantic similarity of wrong RAT answers higher for all three GPT models (p<0.001; e.g. GPT-4o t=-12.02 for human minus model).
limits: Chinese Tencent embedding space.
agent_relevance: Models stay near the cue; distant-association pressure may need external sampling.

source: Orru et al. (2023) Human-like problem-solving abilities in large language models using ChatGPT
finding: ChatGPT on 30 verbal insight problems (15 practice, 15 transfer) with known solution rates from 20 human subjects.
numbers: Global ChatGPT score equalled the most probable human outcome on practice, transfer and combined; its answer pattern was within the 5% most probable human outcomes. Per-item counts not read.
limits: Read abstract only of the PMC page; GPT-3.5 era; problems from Ansburg and Dominowski (2000) may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Old insight sets are probably saturated; this is why new, renewable items matter.

source: Raz et al. (2024) GPT-4 vs humans on verbal insight tasks (as cited in Zhang et al. 2025)
finding: Second-hand: GPT-4 significantly outperformed humans on similar verbal insight tasks.
numbers: not read; no numbers
limits: Original paper not opened; claim only through Zhang et al.
agent_relevance: Treat as unverified.

source: Lin et al. (2025) Sleep-time Compute: Beyond Inference Scaling at Test-time
finding: Closest working machine analogue to incubation: the model thinks offline about a context before any question arrives, then answers faster.
numbers: About 5x less test-time compute for the same accuracy on Stateful GSM-Symbolic and Stateful AIME; scaling sleep-time compute gives up to +13% (GSM-Symbolic) and +18% (AIME) accuracy.
limits: Gains come from pre-computing derived facts for predictable queries; this is not distraction-based incubation and not creative restructuring; math tasks.
agent_relevance: Incubation as free-running distraction failed in humans (schema 4b); the working variant is directed offline preparation. Could be a prepare-the-ledger step.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: when the model tries to stop, append Wait so it re-checks. A forced, external re-look at the impasse.
numbers: AIME24 from 50% to 57% with budget forcing scaling; s1-32B beats o1-preview by up to 27% on MATH and AIME24 (competition math).
limits: Fine-tuned on 1K examples; math only; forced extension can also add errors.
agent_relevance: Matches d'Aliberti: externally triggered re-look helps, spontaneous does not. Cheap operator.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1 (Aha moment in R1-Zero)
finding: The original aha-moment claim: during RL, R1-Zero shows a sudden rise in the word wait during reflection and the authors call it self-evolution.
numbers: One qualitative example (Table 2) and a word-frequency figure; no accuracy comparison of traces with vs without the aha. The paper cites a blog titled There may not be aha moment in r1-zero-like training.
limits: Anecdotal and word-count based; later measured by d'Aliberti and Ribeiro as rare and often harmful.
agent_relevance: Do not treat visible wait as insight.

source: Knoblich, Ohlsson, Haider, Rhenius (1999) Constraint relaxation and chunk decomposition in insight problem solving
finding: Human basis for the NazoNazo framing (constraint relaxation, chunk decomposition); matchstick arithmetic problems. Not opened this session (cited by Mizumoto et al.).
numbers: not read
limits: Background only.
agent_relevance: Source of two operators (relax constraint, split chunk) that a restructure step could name explicitly.

source: Jones (2003) Testing two cognitive theories of insight (ACT-R model of matchstick problems)
finding: Older computational system: an ACT-R model of Knoblich matchstick problems with chunk decomposition and constraint relaxation. From memory, not opened.
numbers: not read
limits: Needs checking before it is cited.
agent_relevance: Shows insight modeled as production-rule change after impasse.
